# Paṭācārātherīgāthā (Thig 5.10)
**ID:** Thig 5.10
**Section:** Therīgāthā (thig)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Paṭācārātherīgāthā* (Thig 5.10) is a canonical poem located in the *Therīgāthā* of the Pali Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. The verses depict the awakening of the nun Paṭācārā, who attains liberation upon retiring to her cell and pulling down the wick of an oil lamp to extinguish its flame [Shaw 2006; Strong 2015]. This vivid episode serves in Buddhist literature as a quintessential illustration of the metaphor connecting meditative release (*nibbāna*) with the extinction of fire [Hayes 2003; Strong 2015].
In the broader canonical tradition, Paṭācārā is celebrated as the foremost bhikkhunī in upholding and mastering monastic discipline (*vinaya*) [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Analayo 2017; Skilling, Eṣā agrā; Collett 2014a]. While later narrative and commentarial traditions dwell extensively on the trauma and grief she suffered prior to encountering the Buddha [Caplow et al. 2013; Williams, Critical Concepts v7], her *Therīgāthā* verses focus on the determination and mindfulness that led directly to her enlightenment [Strong 2015]. Following her liberation, she became a renowned teacher who guided and inspired many other nuns in their meditation practice [Shaw 2006; Strong 2015; Caplow et al. 2013].
